summary: This experimental document defines the PIM Flooding Mechanism and Source Discovery for multicast. It lets sources be discovered by flooding information across the PIM domain, avoiding the need for a Rendezvous Point for that purpose. It is an alternative to relying only on shared trees from an RP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8364 defines a way for PIM routers to share information about active multicast sources. Receivers can join a source tree using that information, but initial packets may be lost while the tree is built.

subtitle: Flood multicast source information so PIM routers can join source trees directly.

tldr.problem: PIM Sparse Mode uses Rendezvous Points and shared trees to introduce new multicast sources to receivers.
tldr.mechanism: Routers flood source-to-group mappings in PIM messages; routers with interested receivers can then join the source tree.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8364 is Experimental and was updated by RFCs 8736 and 9436. It avoids shared trees but drops initial packets while source-tree state is built.

today: RFC 8364 is Experimental and was updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Source Discovery Without a Rendezvous Point
sections.content:
PIM Sparse Mode normally uses a Rendezvous Point and shared tree to introduce packets from a new multicast source to last-hop routers. After learning the source, a last-hop router may join the source's shortest-path tree.

RFC 8364 defines a source-discovery mechanism that floods source information through a PIM domain. It does not require PIM registers, Rendezvous Points, or shared trees. The RFC reports a prototype and limited field testing, while identifying concerns about the processing and state needed as the number of sources grows.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can learn which multicast sources are active from announcements distributed through the PIM domain. They can then join a source tree without first receiving the source's data through a shared tree.

sections.title: The PFM Message and Its TLVs
sections.content:
A PFM message is PIM message type 12. It contains a No-Forward bit, an originator address, and one or more type-length-value (TLV) items. The originator address stays the same as routers forward the message hop by hop; the IP source address changes to the last forwarder.

Each TLV has a transitive bit. A router that does not support a TLV type forwards that TLV only when the bit is set. The originator address must be routable in the domain because routers use it for reverse-path forwarding checks.
sections.plainLanguage: A PFM message carries an originator address and typed information. Routers forward information they do not recognize only when its transitive bit allows forwarding.

sections.title: Sending and Forwarding PFM Messages
sections.content:
A router must not originate more than 6 PFM messages per minute by default, and must leave at least 1000 milliseconds between messages by default. Both limits are configurable. Routers should combine TLVs when practical while keeping messages small enough to avoid IP fragmentation.

A receiver accepts a message only from a directly connected PIM neighbor, addressed to ALL-PIM-ROUTERS, and allowed by administrative boundaries. Unless the No-Forward bit is set for a recently enabled neighbor, the message must come from the reverse-path-forwarding neighbor for its originator. Valid messages are processed and forwarded to PIM-neighbor interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers limit how often they send PFM messages and check their source and direction before processing them. Administrators can configure boundaries that stop all PFM messages or selected information.

sections.title: Announcing Active Sources
sections.content:
The Group Source Holdtime TLV (type 1) carries a multicast group, a source count, a holdtime, and source addresses. A first-hop router announces the source-to-group mapping instead of registering and forwarding the full initial packet to a Rendezvous Point.

While a source is active, its mapping is announced periodically. The default announcement period is 60 seconds and the default holdtime is 210 seconds. A receiving router stores mappings until their holdtime expires and should join advertised source trees for groups with directly connected receivers. Omission from a later message does not remove a mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: A first-hop router announces which source sends to a group. Routers with receivers can use that mapping to join the source tree and keep the mapping until its holdtime expires.

sections.title: Initial Packet Loss and Network Partitions
sections.content:
Unlike the PIM register process, this method does not carry initial source packets to receivers while the source tree is being established. Those packets are dropped until the last-hop router learns about the source and joins the tree. The RFC says this is a poor fit for applications that need initial packets or send only occasional packets, and better suited to steady traffic such as video distribution.

Each network partition can continue distributing mappings and joining sources within that partition. When connectivity returns, periodic announcements share those mappings with the other partitions.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism shares source information, not the first data packets. It can continue within separate network partitions, and routers exchange source mappings again after connectivity returns.

sections.title: Security and Assigned Message Types
sections.content:
PFM messages must come from PIM neighbors, but any router can become a neighbor by sending a Hello. An attacker who forges messages could burden routers or announce many false sources, causing routers to store state and build unnecessary trees.

IPsec can authenticate hop-by-hop PFM messages and protect them from modification. It does not prove that the originator's source information is correct; routers must trust the routers along the path. The RFC registers PIM message type 12 and TLV type 1 for Group Source Holdtime.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication can confirm that a neighbor sent a message, but it cannot prove the original source information is truthful. False announcements can consume router resources.
